analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card companies from raising rates on existing balances and limits surprise fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate; it died in the Banking Committee after being referred on January 14, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend credit card rules to stop issuers from raising interest rates on money you already owe except in narrow cases (like a published index change or a payment more than 30 days late). It would ban double-cycle billing, require 45 days notice before rate increases, cap fees on so-called 'fee harvester' subprime cards, let consumers opt out of over-the-limit fees, require statements at least 25 days before the due date, and bar credit cards for people under 18.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit cardholders, especially people who carry a balance. The bill would protect existing balances from retroactive rate hikes, end billing practices that charge interest on already-paid balances, cut surprise fees, and give clearer statements with more time to pay.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits raising the interest rate on an existing balance except in three narrow cases: a change in a public index, the end or loss of a promotional rate, or a payment more than 30 days late [S2][S3].
Bans double-cycle billing, which charges interest based on balances from earlier billing cycles that were already paid [S2][S3].
Requires 45 days advance written notice before any rate increase takes effect, and statements at least 25 days before the payment due date [S2][S3].

Lets consumers opt out of over-the-limit transactions and fees, limits over-the-limit fees to once per billing cycle, and bars such fees when the limit was exceeded only because of a temporary credit hold [S2][S3].

Stops fees on subprime 'fee harvester' cards from being charged against the card's credit line when first-year fees exceed 25% of the credit limit, and prohibits issuing credit cards to consumers under 18 [S2][S3].

Requires statements to show payoff balance information, creates a presumption that payments mailed 7 days before the due date were on time, and requires payments to be allocated fairly across balances at different rates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks. They would lose the ability to raise rates retroactively on existing balances, collect double-cycle interest, stack over-the-limit fees, and profit from fee-heavy subprime cards — revenue that comes directly out of cardholders' pockets.

drawbacks.text: Restrictions on pricing and fees can lead issuers to recover the money elsewhere, such as higher rates for new customers, annual fees, or tighter credit limits, which can reduce access to credit for riskier borrowers [S2].

The bill still allowed rate increases for late payments, the end of promotional rates, and index changes, so cardholders who missed payments or held promotional-rate cards could still face higher rates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to cardholders — protection from retroactive rate hikes, double-cycle billing, and stacked fees — were substantial and concrete, and the rules carve-outs for genuinely risky behavior were narrow. The main honest cost is that issuers might price the restrictions back in through new fees or tighter credit. On balance the bill's benefits to tens of millions of cardholders outweighed that cost, which is why nearly identical protections became law the same year in the broader Credit CARD Act.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the bill on January 14, 2009, with Senator Udall of Colorado as the only cosponsor listed [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate's entire action on the bill was a single day: introduction, introductory remarks, and referral to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
No markup, committee vote, floor debate, or roll-call ever occurred; the action history ends with the referral [S5].

The bill's core ideas — restrictions on retroactive rate increases, double-cycle billing, over-the-limit fees, and statement timing — closely mirror provisions that did become law later in 2009 in the broader Credit CARD Act, which means cardholders ultimately received most of these protections through other legislation (widely known legislative history, not shown in the provided sources).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers were better off in the short run because this standalone bill never advanced, though cardholders ultimately won many of the same protections through the Credit CARD Act passed later that year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Card issuers, briefly — though Congress passed similar rules anyway

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Cardholders' Bill of Rights Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 2 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators signed on during the two years it sat in committee.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; no action appears in the record after January 14, 2009.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never brought the bill to a markup or vote; pursuing credit card reform through the broader Credit CARD Act instead.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on retroactive rate increases, double-cycle billing, and fees during the 2009 credit card reform debate.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support was two Democratic cosponsors, so the partisan shape of Senate opinion on this bill was never measured.

industries.note: The bill would cut into issuer revenue from retroactive rate increases on existing balances, double-cycle interest, over-the-limit fees, and fee-heavy subprime cards. Those charges are paid by cardholders, so the industry's interest ran directly against consumers'.

The bill would bar charging first-year fees exceeding 25% of the credit limit against the card's own credit line, targeting cards marketed to people with poor credit whose fees ate most of the available credit.
